primary_claim: In a toy MLP autoencoder trained on RGB colors, selectively regularizing (anchoring) just a single concept ('red') to a fixed latent coordinate causes the entire 4D latent space to self-organize predictably around it, forming a color-wheel structure, even under noisy, stochastic (weak) supervision and without constraining the rest of the space.

effect.metric: consistency of resulting latent structure across random initializations (selective vs. curriculum regularization)
effect.value: training on the full color space from the start with selective regularization produced more consistent results across different random initializations than curriculum-learning approaches that gradually introduced complexity

stated_future_work: selective concept suppression: reliably suppress specific colors (e.g. red) at inference time using pre-determined latent directions
concept deletion: modify the network to permanently remove specific capabilities by identifying and ablating relevant weights
apply these techniques to transformer architectures, which present additional challenges due to attention and context-dependent representations
limitations_stated: domain simplicity: color has intrinsic low-dimensional geometric structure that may make it uniquely amenable to this approach, unlike messier higher-dimensional language concepts
architectural simplicity: experiments used tiny MLPs with a few hundred parameters, far simpler than modern language models
unknown trade-offs: there may be significant performance trade-offs between regularized structure and model capabilities
supervision requirements: the technique requires some concept labeling, which is more subjective and challenging for abstract concepts like deception or harmfulness in language models
quote: anchoring even a single concept (red) influences the organization of other concepts, with related concepts clustering nearby — even with weak supervision
